quote: The present analysis identified cardiorespiratory endurance as well as muscular-strength, -endurance, and -power as determinants of sport climbing performance. In contrast, balance, flexibility, and anthropometric characteristics seem to count less.
claim: Climbing-specific muscular strength, muscular endurance and power (and climbing-specific cardiorespiratory endurance) distinguish climbers of different levels; balance, flexibility and anthropometrics matter less.
population: sport climbers of different self-reported levels (74 mostly cross-sectional studies)
used_for: prioritising physical qualities and tests for climbers
caveat: Cross-sectional comparisons show association, not that training a quality causes better climbing.

quote: The overall meta-analysis displayed an improvement in climbing-related test performance following climbing-specific resistance training compared to only climbing (SDM = 0.57, 95%CI = 0.24-0.91).
claim: Adding climbing-specific resistance training (fingerboard, campus board or upper-body resistance training) to climbing improved climbing-specific test performance more than climbing alone, a moderate effect.
population: active climbers in RCTs (5 trials meta-analysed, mostly highly trained men)
used_for: justifying supplementary finger and strength training for intermediate and advanced climbers
caveat: Few small trials, no blinding; outcome is climbing-specific tests, not climbing grade.

quote: finger strength (SDM = 0.41, 95%CI 0.03-0.80), rate of force development (SDM = 0.91, 95%CI = 0.21-1.61), and forearm endurance (SDM = 1.23, 95%CI = 0.69-1.77) were improved by resistance-training of the finger flexors compared to climbing training.
claim: Finger flexor resistance training improved finger strength (small-to-moderate effect), rate of force development and forearm endurance (large effect) more than climbing training alone.
number: finger strength SDM 0.41 (0.03-0.80); RFD SDM 0.91 (0.21-1.61); forearm endurance SDM 1.23 (0.69-1.77)
population: trained climbers in RCTs (finger strength trials: IRCRA grade 18 or higher)

quote: However, the scarcity of studies limits the possibility of recommending specific training methods.
claim: The evidence cannot yet say which specific hangboard or campus protocol is best; it supports adding structured resistance training, not one particular protocol.
used_for: framing protocol choice as preference, not evidence
caveat: Practitioner sources prescribe specific protocols with more confidence than the trials allow.

quote: Each set involved hanging for 10 s with such a load (in terms of extra weight or edge depth, respectively) that allowed a potential hang time of 13 s, leaving a three-second margin before failure. ... This training program consisted of 3 to 5 sets of 10 s dead-hangs with 3 min rest between sets
claim: Maximal hangs (MaxHangs) protocol: 10 s hangs with added weight or a smaller edge chosen so about 13 s would be possible (3 s short of failure), 3 to 5 sets with 3 min rest between sets.
number: 10 s hang at a load allowing 13 s; 3 to 5 sets; 3 min rest

quote: This dead-hang program consisted of 3 to 5 sets of 4 ten-second repetitions each with 5 s rest between repetitions and 1 min rest between sets from week 1 to 4.
claim: Intermittent hangs (IntHangs, a repeater variant) protocol: 3 to 5 sets of 4 ten-second hangs with 5 s rest between hangs and 1 min between sets, on the smallest edge that allows completing the sets, reaching near failure on the last repetition.
number: 3 to 5 sets of 4 ten-second hangs; 5 s rest between hangs; 1 min between sets; weeks 1 to 4

quote: Dead-hang sessions were performed twice a week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, for two 4-week cycles.
claim: In this trial, hangboard sessions were done twice a week over two 4-week cycles.
population: advanced sport climbers who also climbed about 6 days per week

quote: The grip endurance gains and effect size were 34% and 0.6, respectively, for the group following maximal dead-hang training, 45% and 1, respectively, for the group following intermittent dead-hang training, and 7% and 0.1, respectively, for the group applying the combination of both training methods.
claim: After 8 weeks, grip endurance improved 34% with max hangs and 45% with intermittent hangs; the 4 + 4 week combination gained only 7%.
used_for: choosing hang method for endurance goals
caveat: Groups of under 10, more drop-outs in the intermittent groups, differences between groups not statistically significant.

quote: hangboard group HW (Hang weight, + 1.25 kg weight were added each week to hold for a determined time). ... Over the 8-week training period, HW hangboard training significantly improved the climbers' grip strength compared to C [p = 0.032, effect size (ES) 0.36]. ... The overall changes in the HE group did not differ significantly from the C group.
claim: In hangboard-naive intermediate climbers, an 8-week hangboard plan adding 1.25 kg per week improved grip strength more than climbing alone (small effect); a plan that shrank the edge each week did not differ from control.
used_for: progressing added load on the hangboard
caveat: Grip strength measured with a dynamometer, not climbing performance; small sample.

quote: From week three on, an additional + 1.25 kg of weight was added if a hold of 10 s could be accomplished in the last of the three sets.
claim: Load progression rule used in the trial: add 1.25 kg only when the 10 s hang was completed in the last of three sets.
number: +1.25 kg once a 10 s hang is completed in the last set

quote: Frequent low intensity finger loading was as effective at improving grip strength in climbers as training with maximal loads. Additionally, combining low intensity and maximal load training resulted in additive strength gains.
claim: Self-logged app data suggest that frequent low-intensity feet-on hangs improved finger strength about as much as max hangs, and combining both added to the gains.
population: climbers using a training app (n = 526, mostly men), 4-16 week windows
used_for: low-intensity daily hangs as an option
caveat: Retrospective, not randomised, self-reported data, belief effects possible; the protocol designer is a co-author. The low-intensity group's change was not significant against climbing only.

quote: Abrahangs were performed using an edge 18–22 mm deep and the climbers were instructed to keep their feet on the floor at all times (Fig. 1B). Climbers were instructed to keep the intensity low by providing the cue that “only a small strain should be felt in the forearms during the hang”.
claim: Low-intensity hang protocol studied: 18-22 mm edge, feet kept on the floor, intensity cue of only a small strain in the forearms.

quote: Structured low-volume high-resistance training, twice per week hanging from small ledges or a fingerboard, is a feasible approach for climbers.
claim: Expert recommendation: low-volume, high-resistance finger training twice per week on small edges or a fingerboard is a feasible way to add strength training to climbing.

quote: Due to the high mechanical stress and load on the finger flexors, explosive finger and campus board training should be limited in lower-graded climbers.
claim: Expert recommendation: limit explosive finger training and campus boarding in lower-grade climbers because of the high load on the finger flexors.
used_for: gating campus and explosive finger work by level

quote: Stien et al. [36] examined the effects of a five-week campus board training-block in advanced- to elite-level climbers and demonstrated improvement in maximal finger strength, bouldering performance, maximal reach and number of campus board moves to failure, compared with maintaining usual climbing routines.
claim: A five-week campus board block improved finger strength and bouldering performance in advanced-to-elite climbers compared with usual climbing (citing Stien et al. 2021).
used_for: campus board use for advanced climbers only

quote: pooling interventions using muscle contraction intensities higher than 70% of MVC or RM (N = 27) and those using lower intensities (N = 5) resulted in a weighted averaged effect size of tendon stiffness of 0.90 (CI 0.71, 1.08) and 0.04 (CI −0.46, 0.53), respectively.
claim: Tendon stiffness increased with loading above 70% of maximal voluntary contraction but not with lower intensities.
population: healthy adults 18-50 years, Achilles and patellar tendons
used_for: why heavy, controlled finger loading is used to build tissue tolerance
caveat: Lower-limb tendons only; finger tendons and pulleys were not studied. Only 5 low-intensity interventions.

quote: An effective training intervention for the tendon should apply a high loading intensity over a longer intervention duration (>12 weeks).
claim: Tendon adaptation needs high loading intensity sustained over more than 12 weeks.
used_for: length of finger-training phases and patience with progression

quote: Nevertheless, adequate regeneration times and slower adaptation rates of tendon compared to muscle [72-74] should be considered in an exercise intervention to avoid episodes of high tendon strain and stress [75] that may cause maladaptation and tendon damage.
claim: Tendons adapt more slowly than muscle, so training plans need adequate recovery and should avoid spikes of high tendon strain.
used_for: progressing finger load more slowly than strength feels ready for

quote: several of the included studies featuring a duration of 8 weeks found significant adaptations of tendon stiffness [17,25,30], indicating that tendons already respond to increased mechanical loading within 2 months.
claim: Tendons already show measurable stiffness adaptation within about 8 weeks of loading, so adaptation is not only a matter of years.
used_for: counterweight to claims that tendons need years

quote: Avoiding overuse injuries generally requires a methodical and gradual increases in training so that tendon strength can match the loading on newly formed muscles. Muscles can appear in six to ... eight weeks of training, but the tendons may take a minimum of two years to adapt to such training.
claim: UIAA Medical Commission: increase training gradually because muscles adapt in weeks while tendons may need at least two years.
caveat: The two-year figure is an expert estimate with no cited data; Bohm 2015 shows tendon stiffness changes within 8-12 weeks.

quote: Longer but lighter hangs for example 20s but leaving a foot on the floor will help develop strong tendons. Tendons and ligament injuries are very common in climbing. These structures may take 5 times longer to develop than muscular strength.
claim: Practitioner advice for beginners: use lighter, longer hangs (for example 20 s with a foot on the floor); tendons and ligaments may take about 5 times longer to develop than muscle strength.
caveat: The 5-times figure is unsourced practitioner opinion.

quote: Starting with hangboard training too soon is likely to increase your training volume and initially reduce recovery capacity, limiting the quality of your skill acquisition session.
claim: Practitioner advice: beginners should build finger strength mainly by climbing and prioritise skill; starting hangboard training too early adds volume and reduces recovery.
population: beginner climbers in their first year

quote: Have you been climbing and training in a systematized fashion for more than 2 years? Systematized means training or climbing 2-3 days per week
claim: Practitioner readiness criterion for structured dead-hang training: more than 2 years of systematic climbing/training at 2-3 days per week.
number: >2 years of systematic training at 2-3 days per week
caveat: Experience-based threshold, not tested; other practitioners use shorter thresholds.

quote: Check this with the following test on a 25 mm edge (one phalanx and a half): - If you can hang for 15 seconds you could start doing dead-hangs as a method to develop your grip strength.
claim: Practitioner readiness test: if a climber can hang 15 s on a 25 mm edge, dead-hang training can start; below that, build finger strength by climbing.

quote: Are you 16 or older? Are you past your growth spurt? ... The most dangerous period is the growth spurt that takes place at age 11-12 in girls and 13-14 in boys, but the risk remains until the growth plates (the zone where the bones grow) are closed.
claim: Practitioner criterion: intensive dead-hang training only from about 16 years and after the growth spurt; risk is highest during the growth spurt (about 11-12 in girls, 13-14 in boys) and remains until growth plates close.
caveat: Age thresholds differ between sources (16, 16-17, under 18); none is trial-based.

quote: For improving: 2 days/week, 48-72 h recovery between sessions. Maintenance: once you get to a reasonable level, 1 day/week can be enough to keep your gains.
claim: Practitioner dosing: hangboard 2 days per week with 48-72 h between sessions to improve; 1 day per week to maintain.
number: 2 days/week; 48-72 h between sessions; 1 day/week maintenance
population: climbers already suited to hangboard training

quote: Whenever we use a new method, for any level, it is advisable to start with 2 sets to learn the method and/or exercise correctly, controlling the load in a facilitated manner. ... a) 2-3-4-4 in a 4-week cycle ... Week 5 or Weeks 5 & 6: don’t do dead-hangs
claim: Practitioner progression: start any new hang method with 2 sets, build 2-3-4-4 sets over a 4-week cycle, then take 1-2 weeks without dead-hangs before the next cycle.
number: start with 2 sets; 2-3-4-4 sets over a 4-week cycle; no hangs in week 5 or weeks 5 and 6

quote: The average age of the climbers was 14.5 (+/- 0.9) years; 23 were boys, and 1 was a girl. ... All radiographs showed an epiphyseal fracture of the dorsal base of the middle phalanx of the finger; ... An acute injury was not evident in any of the patients. All fractures were thus fatigue fractures caused by repetitive stress.
claim: Epiphyseal fractures at the dorsal base of the finger middle phalanx (middle finger joint) in young climbers were fatigue (stress) fractures without an acute event, mostly in boys around 14-15 years.

quote: Chronic finger pain in young and intensively training climbers must be carefully evaluated, and radiographic studies need to be performed. The risk of epiphyseal injuries must be minimized by eliminating intensive power training in the schedules of athletes of this age.
claim: Chronic finger pain in a young climber needs medical evaluation with imaging; intensive power training should be removed from the training of climbers of this age.
used_for: youth referral trigger and youth training limits

quote: Finger injuries accounted for 52% of all injuries, the shoulder being the second most frequent location. Pulley injuries were the most frequent finger injuries. Of 20 injured young climbers under the age of 15 years, 14 had an epiphyseal fracture
claim: In a large clinic case series, fingers accounted for about half of climbing injuries, pulley injuries were the commonest finger injury, the shoulder came second, and 14 of 20 injured climbers under 15 had an epiphyseal fracture.
number: fingers 52%; 14 of 20 injured climbers under 15 years had an epiphyseal fracture
population: 836 patients with 911 injuries at one German climbing-medicine clinic, 2009-2012

quote: 82% of the injuries affected the upper extremity and the most frequent injury was PPSI (45.3% of all injuries).
claim: In injured adolescent climbers, 82% of injuries were upper-limb and primary periphyseal stress injuries of the fingers were the most frequent diagnosis (45.3%).
population: 95 injured climbers under 18 at a referral centre (2017-2020)
caveat: Referral-centre sample over-represents chronic injuries.

quote: PPSIs typically present during periods of accelerated growth velocity, around 13–15 years of age, predominantly affecting males, and most commonly affecting the middle and ring fingers.
claim: Finger growth-plate stress injuries typically appear during the growth spurt, around 13-15 years, mostly in boys and in the middle and ring fingers.

quote: Reducing the use of the finger crimp grip, monitoring the load, ensuring adequate recovery and targeted education appear to be crucial.
claim: For adolescents: reduce crimp-grip use, monitor training load, ensure adequate recovery and educate athletes, parents and coaches.

quote: We advise that climbers aged under 18 do not campus feet-off or dynamically. While you are growing, you are at serious risk of injuring the growth plates in your fingers as they will not be fused yet. ... Younger climbers benefit more from improving their flexibility, co-ordination and technique.
claim: BMC guidance approved by the UIAA Medical Commission: climbers under 18 should not campus feet-off or dynamically because finger growth plates are not yet fused; young climbers gain more from flexibility, coordination and technique.
caveat: Expert guidance without trial data; many coaches use campus boards with some adolescents.

quote: Don’t use a campus board with your feet off, or dynamically, unless you are an experienced climber and fully understand what you are doing Warm up properly, especially the fingers Use the campus board at the beginning of your training session – tiredness increases your risk of injury
claim: For adults: campus feet-off or dynamically only if experienced, warm up the fingers first, and campus at the start of the session because fatigue raises injury risk.

quote: If any campus board training is done, it should only be undertaken by veteran climbers (i.e. climbing around 8 to 10 years), and not those aged up to around 16 or 17 as their fingers are still growing.
claim: UIAA Medical Commission: campus training only for veteran climbers with about 8-10 years of climbing, and not for those aged up to about 16-17.
number: 8 to 10 years of climbing; not up to age 16 or 17
caveat: Stricter than other guidance; based on expert opinion; trials of campus training used advanced-to-elite adults.

quote: The limited amount of studies on the fingers of dedicated young climbers suggest training intensity should be reduced during the adolescent growth spurt to reduce the risk of fractures to the growth plates in the fingers, and other possible finger/s damage. The final growth spurt is around age 13 to 15.
claim: Reduce finger training intensity during the adolescent growth spurt (around 13-15 years) to lower growth-plate fracture risk.

quote: By regularly plotting a child/adolescent’s growth on height and weight charts (i.e. every three months), their developmental growth is clear. If they outgrow their clothes or shoes, growth should be plotted more often, and training adjusted during this period if they are dedicated sports people. If your child’s height or weight drops two percentiles (growth lines) on these charts, they may need specialist referrals
claim: Plot a young climber's height and weight about every three months, adjust training during fast growth, and refer if height or weight drops two percentile lines.

quote: Forty-six coaches (63%) reported using full weight (no foot contact) campus board training in some or all of their climbers. ... Climbing coaches in the United States disagree on the use of campus board training in adolescent climbers.
claim: Most surveyed US youth-team coaches (63%) used feet-off campus training with some adolescents, and coaches disagree about who can do it safely.
used_for: documenting that campus use in youth is contested

quote: The three most frequent sites of injury were fingers (41.3%), shoulders (19.4%) and elbows (17.7%).
claim: Among climbers reporting chronic injuries, the most common sites were fingers (41.3%), shoulders (19.4%) and elbows (17.7%).

quote: Higher climbing intensity, bouldering, reduced grip/finger strength, use of a “crimp” grip, and previous injury were associated with an increased risk of overuse injury. Additionally, a strength training intervention prevented shoulder and elbow injuries. BMI/body weight, warm up/cool downs, stretching, taping and hydration were not associated with risk of overuse injury.
claim: Overuse-injury risk in adult climbers is associated with higher climbing intensity, bouldering, lower finger strength, crimp-grip use and previous injury; body weight, warm-up, stretching and taping were not associated with risk.
caveat: Mostly cross-sectional and retrospective studies; associations, not causes.

quote: Injuries present with pain and swelling over the affected pulley, and patients may feel or hear a pop at the time of injury. Sequential pulley ruptures are required for clinical bowstringing of the flexor tendons.
claim: Pulley rupture signs: pain and swelling over the affected pulley, often a felt or heard pop at the time of injury; visible bowstringing of the flexor tendons indicates multiple ruptured pulleys.

quote: This is something you cannot answer for yourself, go and see a physician preferably one that has an understanding of climbing injuries. But if you suddenly loaded the finger and heard/felt a pop it is quite possible, particularly if the finger swells afterward, this warrants investigation
claim: A sudden finger load with a heard or felt pop, especially with later swelling, warrants assessment by a physician experienced with climbing injuries; the climber cannot self-diagnose it.
used_for: referral trigger for suspected pulley or tendon rupture

quote: Classically it is pain some time after activity, then pain at the start and then after activity, then pain during and after, then pain all the time. Not all overuse injuries manifest themselves this way but many do. Whatever the case do not wait until you have pain all the time!
claim: Overuse injuries often progress from pain after climbing, to pain at the start and after, to pain during and after, to constant pain; do not wait until pain is constant before seeing a doctor.
used_for: overuse warning signs and referral timing

quote: There can be many reasons for shoulder pain, and the cause needs a proper medical diagnosis and treatment.
claim: Shoulder pain in climbers has many possible causes and needs medical diagnosis rather than coach management.

quote: Two RCTs conducted on the same study cohort, reported that closed chain eccentric and strength exercises performed 3–4 times per week for one year, could reduce the likelihood of shoulder injuries (30) and elbow injuries (31)
claim: One trial cohort showed that closed-chain eccentric and strength exercises 3-4 times per week for a year reduced shoulder and elbow injuries in climbers.
number: 3-4 times per week for one year
caveat: Single cohort, small sample; does not apply to finger injuries.

quote: However, the results of the two included studies in this review had a relatively small sample size (n = 84) focusing on injuries of the elbows and shoulders (30, 31). Correspondingly, these findings cannot be applied to injuries of the fingers
claim: The only prevention trial in climbers was small and covered shoulders and elbows, so no tested programme exists for preventing finger injuries.

quote: Many overuse injuries are the result of muscle imbalances such as over development of some muscles, while neglecting other muscles like shoulder rotator cuff or forearm extensor muscles.
claim: UIAA Medical Commission view: many overuse injuries result from muscle imbalances, such as neglected rotator cuff or forearm extensor muscles.
caveat: Expert opinion; the imbalance mechanism has not been tested in climbing trials.

quote: Each warm-up session lasted 10 minutes. ... All warm-ups increased the maximal muscle strength of the elbow flexors and shoulder extensors, but did not in finger flexors.
claim: Ten-minute warm-ups (dynamic band stretching, vibration rolling or climbing-specific) improved shoulder range of motion and elbow/shoulder strength but did not increase finger flexor strength.

quote: The warm-up routine before the test started with general mobilisation of the neck, shoulders, arms, wrists, and fingers, continuing with a specific segment of 3-5 sets of dead-hangs on a medium edge depth (15-20 mm), progressing from 10 to 20 s.
claim: Warm-up used before maximal finger testing in a trial: general mobilisation of neck to fingers, then 3-5 progressive hangs on a 15-20 mm edge lasting 10 to 20 s.
caveat: A protocol description, not a test of whether this warm-up improves strength or prevents injury.

quote: However, based upon data from four studies (8, 18, 28, 32), two of which were prospective studies (8, 18), both warming up or cooling down had no protective effect against overuse injuries.
claim: Observational data show no protective association between warming up or cooling down and overuse injury in climbers.

quote: a proper warm up at the beginning of the session and warm down with stretching at end of climb session - including the forearms and fingers - will aid recovery, maintain proper limb functioning, and help prevent injury.
claim: UIAA Medical Commission view: a proper warm-up including forearms and fingers helps prevent injury.

quote: Forty-three sport lead climbers reported a score of 20 or above on the EAT-26 indicating an 8.6% prevalence of DE in this sample. Male climbers had a DE prevalence of 6.3% (24 of 383) and female climbers more than doubled that with 16.5% (19 of 115).
claim: Screening-questionnaire disordered eating was found in 8.6% of international sport lead climbers: 6.3% of men and 16.5% of women.
number: 8.6% overall; men 6.3%; women 16.5% (EAT-26 score 20 or above)
population: 498 international sport lead climbers, web survey
caveat: Self-selected sample, screening tool only, no control group.

quote: There were no differences between rock-climbers and controls regarding ED symptoms. Symptoms were higher among female rock-climbers (26%) than male (5.8%).
claim: Advanced and elite Swedish climbers did not have more eating-disorder symptoms than controls, but symptoms were much more common in female (26%) than male (5.8%) climbers.

quote: Notably, a recent survey examining amenorrhea and eating disorders among female competing climbers found that 18.5% (18 out of 114) reported amenorrhea
claim: In a survey of female competitive climbers, 18.5% reported amenorrhea (citing Joubert et al. 2022).

quote: Coaches should address and monitor BMI and screening of amenorrhea and disordered eating in climbers.
claim: Coaches should screen climbers for amenorrhea and disordered eating.

quote: There are no scientific studies to prove that losing weight will automatically make you a better climber.
claim: No studies show that losing weight automatically improves climbing.

quote: It is a smarter and healthier option to build up sport-specific strength and endurance (ie powerful forearms) for both health and performance, rather than losing weight quickly or maintaining low energy diets.
claim: Build sport-specific strength and endurance rather than losing weight quickly or maintaining low-energy diets.
used_for: redirecting weight-loss goals to strength goals

quote: Among the possible grip types, the half-crimp type was chosen for testing as well as for training given that it is the most widely used grip on small edges in climbing (Schweizer, 2001) and is safer than the full crimp.
claim: The hangboard trials used the half-crimp grip for training, as the most common small-edge grip and safer than the full crimp (authors' rationale citing Schweizer 2001).
caveat: A stated rationale, not a tested comparison of grip safety.

quote: A maximal dead-hangs workout (MaxHangs, see the glossary here) should always be the first content of the session.
claim: Practitioner advice: do maximal hangs first in the session, when fresh.

quote: The results showed (a) positive effects of strength training on all variables, (b) a trend toward a mixture of MS and HYP or END training, (c) a trend toward semispecific exercise, and (d) similar effects for dynamic and static exercise with a trend toward a mixture of both.
claim: A systematic review of controlled climbing studies found positive effects of strength training on climbing performance, grip strength, upper-limb strength endurance, strength and power, with trends favouring a mix of maximal-strength and hypertrophy or endurance training, semispecific exercises, and a mix of static and dynamic exercise.
caveat: trends only; small, heterogeneous studies

quote: Coaches and athletes are recommended to combine static and dynamic semispecific exercises in a HYP and MS or END training.
claim: The review authors recommend combining static and dynamic semispecific exercises in hypertrophy, maximal-strength or endurance training blocks.
caveat: authors' recommendation from low-quality evidence

quote: 10 weeks of HBT in addition to regular climbing was highly effective for increasing maximal finger strength compared with continuing regular climbing training for intermediate and advanced climbers.
claim: In intermediate to advanced climbers, 10 weeks of hangboard training (two sessions per week) added to normal climbing increased maximal finger strength more than climbing alone.
population: 35 intermediate to advanced climbers (8 women, 27 men)
caveat: unblinded; strength tests, not climbing grade

quote: At post-test, the HBT group demonstrated 17, 18, 28, 10, 11, and 12% improvement in peak force, average force, RFD in 23 mm rung condition, average force in jug condition, utilization rate in peak force, and dead-hang duration, respectively
claim: In the hangboard group peak force rose 17%, average force 18%, rate of force development 28% and dead-hang duration 12% on the 23 mm rung test; rate of force development and dead-hang duration did not differ significantly from the control group.
caveat: between-group differences were significant for peak and average force only

quote: Participants trained on a 12 mm-deep hold, twice a week for 4 weeks.
claim: In a 4-week trial, experienced climbers trained twice a week on a 12 mm hold at 100% of maximal finger strength, or intermittent repetitions at 80% or at 60%.

quote: A significantly improved MFS was observed in the F100 and F80 groups but not in the F60 group. Significantly higher stamina and endurance measurements were observed in the F80 and F60 groups but not in the F100 group.
claim: Maximal finger strength improved in the 100% and 80% groups but not the 60% group, while stamina and endurance improved in the 80% and 60% groups but not the 100% group; the intensity chosen shapes which quality improves, with 80% improving both.
caveat: 4 weeks only; supports matching intensity to goal, not a single best protocol

quote: Sixteen advanced-to-elite climbers were randomly allocated to two (TG2), or four weekly campus board training sessions (TG4), or a control group (CG).
claim: A randomised trial compared two and four weekly campus-board sessions with normal climbing in advanced-to-elite lead climbers.

quote: whereas TG2 improved bouldering performance (ES = 2.59, p = 0.016) and maximal moves to failure on the campus board more than CG (ES = 1.65, p = 0.008). No differences between the training groups were found (p = 0.107-1.000).
claim: Two weekly campus-board sessions improved bouldering performance (effect size 2.59) and campus moves to failure more than the control group, and two and four weekly sessions did not differ significantly from each other.
caveat: tiny sample; adults only; do not extend to lower-grade climbers or youth (see CLB-34, CLB-36)

quote: The largest amount of bowstringing was caused by the flexor digitorum profundus tendon in the crimp grip position being less using slope grip position (PIP joint extended).
claim: Tendon bowstringing, which loads the finger pulleys, was largest in the crimp grip and smaller in the slope grip with the middle finger joint extended.
population: 16 fingers of 4 climbers, measured in vivo
caveat: very small measurement study

quote: During a warm-up, the distance of bowstringing over the distal edge of the A2 pulley increased by 0.6mm (30%) and was loaded about 3 times the force applied at the fingertip during crimp grip position. Load up to 116N was measured over the A2 pulley.
claim: In the crimp grip the A2 pulley carried about 3 times the force applied at the fingertip, with loads up to 116N measured, and bowstringing over the A2 pulley increased by 0.6mm (30%) during a warm-up.
number: 0.6mm (30%) increase; about 3 times fingertip force; up to 116N
caveat: explains why crimp use and warm-up matter, not an injury-risk threshold

quote: In climbers with 6 y or more in the sport, SPIIF was not common and RFT was negatively associated with SPIIF (χ2 [1, n=200]=4.57; P=0.03). In contrast to this, in male climbers who had been climbing for less than 6 y and had advanced to 7a level or higher (French lead/Font bouldering), SPIIF was common and RFT was positively associated with SPIIF
claim: In a survey of Finnish climbers, regular fingerboard training was linked to less finger pain in climbers with 6 or more years of climbing but to more finger pain in male climbers with under 6 years of climbing who had reached 7a or higher.
number: 6 y or more; less than 6 y; 7a or higher
population: 434 Finnish climbers (survey); 200 with 6 years or more
caveat: cross-sectional survey, cannot show cause; supports caution for fast-progressing newer climbers

quote: In total, 149 physeal stress injuries occurred in 98 adolescent climbers with a mean age of 14 years and range of 10 to 18 years. A total of 146 injuries (98%) occurred at the proximal interphalangeal joint.
claim: In a scoping review, 149 physeal stress injuries were reported in 98 adolescent climbers (mean age 14 years, range 10 to 18), 98% of them at the proximal interphalangeal (middle finger) joint.
number: 149 injuries; 98 climbers; mean age 14 years; 98% at the proximal interphalangeal joint
caveat: case series, so no incidence rate

quote: Overall, return to sport time ranged from 2 weeks to 6 months, and 91% were able to return to climbing.
claim: After a finger growth plate injury, return to sport took 2 weeks to 6 months, and 91% of adolescent climbers returned to climbing.
caveat: outcome information only; management belongs to the treating physician
